claim: Humans share with other animals basic numerical capacities.
source: Humans share with other animals basic numerical capacities (Cantlon and Brannon, 2007; Cordes et al., 2001; Cordes and Brannon, 2009; Rugani, 2018; Vallortigara, 2018); this evolutionarily ancient number sense serves as a building block for our unique mathematical abilities (Dehaene, 2011).

evidence: This is supported by citation to Dehaene's work on the evolution of mathematical cognition.

claim: The mental number line is an association of small numbers with the left and large ones with the right.
source: A distinctive feature of the human numerical system is the mental number line (MNL): an association of small numbers with the left and large ones with the right.
evidence: This is a well-established definition in the numerical cognition literature.

claim: Numeral visualization in various spatial configurations (right-to-left, circular, and vertical) was first reported by Galton, 1880.
source: Numeral visualization in various spatial configurations (right-to-left, circular, and vertical) was first reported by Galton, 1880 (see also Abbadie (d'), 1880; Seron et al., 1992; Tang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a historical claim supported by citation to Galton's original work.

claim: The first experimental demonstration of left-to-right numerical spatialization was observed in a parity judgment task.
source: The first experimental demonstration of left-to-right numerical spatialization was observed in a parity judgment task, where participants pressed a left or right key for odd or even numerals.
evidence: This refers to the classic SNARC effect study.

claim: Faster responses to small numbers on the left and to large numbers on the right have been described as the SNARC effect.
source: Faster responses to small numbers on the left and to large numbers on the right have been described as the SNARC effect (spatial-numerical association of response codes): a spatial congruency between the response side (left or right) and the relative position of the represented numerical magnitude on an oriented MNL (left space/small numbers and right space/large numbers) (Dehaene et al., 1993).
evidence: This is the definition of the SNARC effect, supported by citation to the original study.

claim: Left-to-right numerical spatialization has been replicated across various experiments.
source: Left-to-right numerical spatialization has been replicated across various experiments (e.g. Bächtold et al., 1998; Dehaene, 2011); however, evidence remains inconsistent across paradigms (Karolis et al., 2011) and reading direction (Shaki et al., 2009; Zebian, 2005), emphasizing the role of task-dependent factors and culture in shaping numerical spatialization.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to replication studies.

claim: Evidence for left-to-right numerical spatialization remains inconsistent across paradigms.
source: Left-to-right numerical spatialization has been replicated across various experiments (e.g. Bächtold et al., 1998; Dehaene, 2011); however, evidence remains inconsistent across paradigms (Karolis et al., 2011) and reading direction (Shaki et al., 2009; Zebian, 2005), emphasizing the role of task-dependent factors and culture in shaping numerical spatialization.

claim: Spatial biases in numerical processing have been reported in young infants.
source: Moreover, spatial biases in numerical processing that demonstrated spatial-numerical association (SNA) have been reported in young infants (Bulf et al., 2016; de Hevia, 2021; de Hevia and Spelke, 2010; Rugani et al., 2022; West and McCrink, 2021), newborns (de Hevia et al., 2014; de Hevia et al., 2017; Di Giorgio et al., 2019; McCrink et al., 2020), and nonhumans (Drucker and Brannon, 2014; Giurfa et al., 2022; Rugani et al., 2015a; Rugani et al., 2010; Rugani et al., 2024; Rugani et al., 2007; Rugani et al., 2020b), challenging the predominant role of culture in determining the left-to-right orientation.

claim: Evidence in nonhuman animals challenges the predominant role of culture in determining the left-to-right orientation of numerical spatialization.
source: Moreover, spatial biases in numerical processing that demonstrated spatial-numerical association (SNA) have been reported in young infants (Bulf et al., 2016; de Hevia, 2021; de Hevia and Spelke, 2010; Rugani et al., 2022; West and McCrink, 2021), newborns (de Hevia et al., 2014; de Hevia et al., 2017; Di Giorgio et al., 2019; McCrink et al., 2020), and nonhumans (Drucker and Brannon, 2014; Giurfa et al., 2022; Rugani et al., 2015a; Rugani et al., 2010; Rugani et al., 2024; Rugani et al., 2007; Rugani et al., 2020b), challenging the predominant role of culture in determining the left-to-right orientation.

claim: Nervous systems across various species are prewired in how they relate numbers to space.
source: Evidence in nonhuman animals indicates that nervous systems across various species, despite their different levels of complexity, are prewired in how they relate numbers to space.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparative evidence of SNA across species.

claim: Numerical spatialization likely originates from neural bases, yet it remains flexible and subject to modulation by experience and contextual factors.
source: Together, conflicting evidence of an oriented representation of numerical magnitude, as described in the MNL in humans, and broader spatial biases in numerical processing, as reported in the SNA in nonverbal or preverbal subjects, suggests that numerical spatialization likely originates from neural bases, yet it remains flexible and subject to modulation by experience and contextual factors (Rugani and de Hevia, 2017).
evidence: This is a synthesis of the conflicting evidence, suggesting both innate and learned components.

claim: The first evidence of numerical spatialization in nonhuman subjects was observed in day-old domestic chicks.
source: The first evidence of numerical spatialization in nonhuman subjects was observed in day-old domestic chicks (Rugani et al., 2007; Rugani et al., 2010) and adult Clark's nutcrackers (Rugani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a historical claim supported by citations to the original studies.

claim: The first evidence of numerical spatialization in nonhuman subjects was observed in adult Clark's nutcrackers.
source: The first evidence of numerical spatialization in nonhuman subjects was observed in day-old domestic chicks (Rugani et al., 2007; Rugani et al., 2010) and adult Clark's nutcrackers (Rugani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a historical claim supported by citations to the original studies.

claim: Birds learned to identify a target item, e.g., the 4th, in a sagittally oriented array of identical items.
source: Birds learned to identify a target item, e.g., the 4th, in a sagittally oriented array of identical items.
evidence: This describes the experimental paradigm used in previous studies.

claim: When tested with the array rotated by 90°, animals selected the 4th left item more often than the 4th right one.
source: They were then tested with the array rotated by 90°, thus laying on a fronto-parallel plane with the items oriented left to right. Animals selected the 4th left item more often than the 4th right one, suggesting that number is intrinsically represented from left to right (Rugani et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the key finding from previous studies using this paradigm.

claim: The left-to-right proto-counting tendency has been observed in adult rhesus monkeys.
source: Using this paradigm, the same left-to-right proto-counting tendency has also been observed in adult rhesus monkeys (Drucker and Brannon, 2014) and preschoolers (West and McCrink, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on rhesus monkeys.

claim: The left-to-right proto-counting tendency has been observed in preschoolers.
source: Using this paradigm, the same left-to-right proto-counting tendency has also been observed in adult rhesus monkeys (Drucker and Brannon, 2014) and preschoolers (West and McCrink, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on preschoolers.

source: Concurrently, specific neurons responding to numerosities have been identified in human (Pearson et al., 2009; Piazza et al., 2004; Piazza and Eger, 2016), monkey (Nieder et al., 2002), crow (Ditz and Nieder, 2015), and chick (Kobylkov et al., 2022) brains.

source: The right hemisphere is specialized for analyzing spatial information (Rashid and Andrew, 1989; Regolin et al., 2005) and for processing numerical information (Piazza and Eger, 2016; Rugani and Regolin, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on hemispheric specialization.

source: The right hemisphere is specialized for analyzing spatial information (Rashid and Andrew, 1989; Regolin et al., 2005) and for processing numerical information (Piazza and Eger, 2016; Rugani and Regolin, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on hemispheric specialization.

claim: Functional overlap between spatial and numerical processing has been proposed as the basis for the SNA.
source: This functional overlap (Harvey et al., 2013; Zorzi et al., 2002) has been proposed as the basis for the SNA that prompts animals to start counting from left to right.
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical papers on the overlap between spatial and numerical cognition.

claim: The right-hemisphere dominance model proposes that functional overlap between spatial and numerical processing prompts animals to start counting from left to right.
source: This functional overlap (Harvey et al., 2013; Zorzi et al., 2002) has been proposed as the basis for the SNA that prompts animals to start counting from left to right. This will be referred to as the right-hemisphere dominance model (Rugani et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes one of the theoretical models being tested in the study.

claim: The emotional valence model is grounded in evidence demonstrating that the right hemisphere processes negative emotions and the left hemisphere handles positive ones.
source: The emotional valence model is grounded in evidence demonstrating that the right hemisphere processes negative emotions and the left hemisphere handles positive ones (Davidson, 2004; Vallortigara, 2018).
evidence: This describes the basis of the emotional valence model, supported by citations.

claim: The emotional valence model posits that small numerosities are associated with a negative valence and activate the right hemisphere that directs movement toward the left.
source: This model posits that small numerosities are associated with a negative valence and activate the right hemisphere that directs movement toward the left; large numerosities would be associated with a positive valence, activating the left hemisphere that leads movement toward the right (Vallortigara, 2018).
evidence: This describes the predictions of the emotional valence model, supported by citation.

claim: The emotional valence model posits that large numerosities are associated with a positive valence and activate the left hemisphere that leads movement toward the right.
source: This model posits that small numerosities are associated with a negative valence and activate the right hemisphere that directs movement toward the left; large numerosities would be associated with a positive valence, activating the left hemisphere that leads movement toward the right (Vallortigara, 2018).
evidence: This describes the predictions of the emotional valence model, supported by citation.

claim: BAFT links spatial frequency processing to higher cognitive functions.
source: BAFT links spatial frequency processing to higher cognitive functions.

source: The right hemisphere specializes in processing low spatial frequencies, while the left hemisphere, high spatial frequencies (Gazzaniga, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to research on hemispheric specialization for spatial frequency.

claim: Smaller numerosities correspond to low frequencies, and large numerosities to high frequencies.
source: Because smaller numerosities correspond to low frequencies, and large numerosities to high frequencies, such hemispheric specialization may explain SNA (Felisatti et al., 2020).

claim: Lateralization levels in domestic chicks can be easily manipulated by controlling exposure to light in the final period of incubation, between embryonic days 18 and 21.
source: As for the first aim, lateralization levels in domestic chicks can be easily manipulated by controlling exposure to light in the final period of incubation, between embryonic days 18 and 21 (Rogers and Bolden, 1991; Rogers and Sink, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on light-induced lateralization in chicks.

claim: During development, the embryo rotates such that the right eye faces outward toward the translucent eggshell and any available environmental light.
source: During development, the embryo rotates such that the right eye faces outward toward the translucent eggshell and any available environmental light. In contrast, the left eye is oriented toward the body, receiving little to no light.
evidence: This describes the natural developmental process in chick embryos.

claim: The left eye is oriented toward the body, receiving little to no light during chick embryo development.

source: Egg exposure to light leads to an asymmetrical stimulation of the two eyes such that there is an increase in forebrain projections from the left side of the thalamus (fed by the light-stimulated right eye) compared with the right side (Deng and Rogers, 1998).

claim: The right visual Wulst receives more bilateral information from the two eyes than the left one.

source: Evidence shows that as little as 2 hr light exposure prior to hatching is sufficient to induce these brain asymmetries (Deng and Rogers, 1997; Rogers, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies on light exposure.

source: As a consequence of light-enhanced hemispheric differentiation, light-incubated chicks, Li-chicks, are strongly lateralized, as demonstrated by cognitive and behavioral biases (Daisley et al., 2009).

source: For the present study, we expect that Li-chicks will exhibit a clearer left-to-right oriented numerical spatialization compared to dark-incubated chicks, Di-chicks, whose brain lateralization is mainly prevented (Rogers and Bolden, 1991).
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study, based on previous research on light-induced lateralization.

source: Strongly lateralized chicks perform better in dual tasks requiring simultaneous foraging and predator monitoring (Dharmaretnam and Rogers, 2005), in discrimination and categorization tasks such as distinguishing pebbles from food grains (Deng and Rogers, 1997), and in transitive inference tasks where they learn hierarchical stimulus relationships (A>B>C>D>E) that then apply to novel pairings (i.e. AE and BD) (Daisley et al., 2010).

claim: Brain lateralization seems to improve numerical ability.
source: Brain lateralization also seems to improve numerical ability: strongly lateralized fish outperform non-lateralized individuals in quantity discrimination tasks.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent description of fish studies.

claim: Strongly lateralized fish outperform non-lateralized individuals in quantity discrimination tasks.
source: Brain lateralization also seems to improve numerical ability: strongly lateralized fish outperform non-lateralized individuals in quantity discrimination tasks. In a shoal-choice task, non-lateralized fish failed to distinguish between four and six conspecifics, while lateralized fish reliably selected the larger group. Similarly, in an abstract dot discrimination task, lateralized fish successfully distinguished between three and four dots, whereas non-lateralized fish did not (Dadda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to research on fish lateralization and numerical cognition.

claim: In a shoal-choice task, non-lateralized fish failed to distinguish between four and six conspecifics, while lateralized fish reliably selected the larger group.

evidence: This is supported by citation to research on fish lateralization and numerical cognition.

source: Although lateralization was inferred indirectly through the mirror test, similar results in shoal-choice tasks emerged using a detour test (Gatto et al., 2019), supporting the hypothesis that brain lateralization enhances cognitive efficiency and was a key selective force in evolution (Dadda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to research on lateralization in fish.
